note: basil in a windowsill pot, the new leaves lighter at the top
shortInsight: A plant's newest leaves often start out lighter or redder and darken as they harden.
physicalAction: Find the newest leaves at the tip and the oldest leaf lower down. Hold your hand near each — which is softer?
nextMission: Compare the newest and oldest leaf on one plant.

note: a hedge along the path with two clearly different leaf edges
shortInsight: Leaf edges follow rules: smooth, toothed and lobed edges belong to different plant strategies.
physicalAction: Trace one leaf's edge with your eyes — smooth, toothed, or lobed? Then find a neighbouring leaf with a different edge.
nextMission: Find two leaves with different edge shapes.

note: daisies open in the lawn, a few still closed
shortInsight: Flowers are working: petals advertise, and nectar is the payment.
physicalAction: Watch this flower for one quiet minute. Note every visitor and how long each one stays.
nextMission: Count flower visits for one minute.

note: a row of sunflowers leaning different ways
shortInsight: Flowers can face different directions for practical reasons — light, shelter, or passing pollinators.
physicalAction: Find a second flower of the same kind. Note which way each one faces and whether one side is more sheltered.
nextMission: Compare which way two flowers face.

note: a young tree and a very old one standing side by side
shortInsight: Bark records age: young trunks are usually smoother than old ones of the same kind.
physicalAction: Compare the two trunks at eye level, then turn your cheek away and look again from the corner of your eye — what shows now?
nextMission: Compare bark on a young and an old tree.

note: a big tree dropping small cases onto the path
shortInsight: Trees leave clues at their base — seeds, cones, catkins or fruit — often before you think to look up.
physicalAction: Look at the ground under this tree and find one thing it dropped. Then look up and find where it came from.
nextMission: Match one thing on the ground to the branch it fell from.

note: a line of trees between open sun and shade
shortInsight: Trees cool the air around them; walking between them, you can feel the change on your skin.
physicalAction: Walk a slow line from open sun into tree shade and back. Note exactly where the air changes.
nextMission: Find the line where sun becomes shade.

note: a repeated two-note call from somewhere in the hedge
shortInsight: Birds repeat themselves — calls are patterns, not noise.
physicalAction: Close your eyes and listen for one call. Wait for it to repeat twice before you open your eyes.
nextMission: Learn one bird's call pattern by ear.

note: a busy feeding flock that scattered when people passed
shortInsight: Birds settle back into their routine about a minute after the loudest disturbance passes.
physicalAction: Stand still where you are for ninety seconds without moving. Note the first bird to return to the hedge.
nextMission: Time how long until birds resume after quiet returns.

note: a small bird perched low over the water
shortInsight: A photograph of behaviour beats a photograph of a species — context tells the story.
physicalAction: Frame one photo that includes where the bird is, not just the bird. Then lower the phone and watch it resume.
nextMission: Take one photo that shows where the bird lives.

note: a small beetle on a leaf, motionless
shortInsight: An insect on a plant is usually eating, resting, hunting, or passing through — its posture tells you which.
physicalAction: Watch from where you stand, hands away, and decide which of the four your beetle is doing.
nextMission: Classify the insect's behaviour from a respectful distance.

note: ants running a line along the edge of the paving
shortInsight: Many small insects pause when the world moves and resume when it stops.
physicalAction: Stand absolutely still for one minute. Watch whether the line resumes at the same pace.
nextMission: Stay still until the ants forget you.

note: a rabbit at the far edge of the field, ears up
shortInsight: Wild animals notice you long before you notice them — their reaction measures the distance.
physicalAction: Stop where you are and watch what the animal does next: freeze, move away, or carry on. That is your distance limit.
nextMission: Let the animal decide how close is close enough.

note: a deer pausing at the treeline before it moves off
shortInsight: Animals share this place with you; their behaviour is a language of comfort and alarm.
physicalAction: Keep your distance and note which direction the animal moves and whether it keeps you in view.
nextMission: Sketch the animal's direction of travel in your mind — in, out, or around.

note: a pale fungus growing from the side of a mossy trunk
shortInsight: Fungi are the visible edge of networks that run under your feet; some harmless-looking species mimic dangerous ones.
physicalAction: From where you stand, note exactly what the fungus grows on: wood, soil, or moss. Keep your hands away.
nextMission: Record what a fungus grows on — wood, soil, or moss.

note: a small cap in the grass after several damp days
shortInsight: A fungus appears only when conditions align — damp, warmth, and something to decompose.
physicalAction: Stand a step back and describe the conditions around it: how damp, how shaded, what it grows from. Keep your hands away.
nextMission: Describe the conditions one fungus chose.

note: two stones that look identical, one in sun and one under a tree
shortInsight: Wet rock shows colour that dry rock hides.
physicalAction: Hover your hand above each stone and compare warmth. Then check for the one difference in colour.
nextMission: Compare a sunlit and a shaded rock.

note: a gravel path with one stone that does not match
shortInsight: Every path is made of local stone; the surface underfoot is a geological sample.
physicalAction: Walk twenty steps watching only the ground. Find one stone that does not match the path.
nextMission: Find one stone that travelled — or was carried — to this path.

note: fields stacked behind each other into the distance
shortInsight: Landscapes are layered: foreground, middle ground, skyline.
physicalAction: Walk twenty steps and stop. Name one thing in each layer — near, middle, far — in that order.
nextMission: Name the three layers of this view.

note: a still evening in the park, almost no wind
shortInsight: Sound maps a landscape: water, wind and birds each arrive from their own direction.
physicalAction: Turn slowly through one full circle. Point at the loudest direction, then the quietest.
nextMission: Map the loudest and quietest directions around you.

note: rough stone wall beside a smooth metal railing
shortInsight: Texture is light: the same surface changes with the angle you view it from.
physicalAction: Look at this surface from three angles. Which angle reveals the most detail?
nextMission: Find the angle that reveals the most texture.

note: rough bark beside a polished bench end
shortInsight: Rough surfaces trap scent and moisture; smooth ones shed them.
physicalAction: Compare the two surfaces with the back of your hand — one finger, gentle. Which stays cooler?
nextMission: Compare one rough and one smooth surface in two places.

note: thin cloud moving while the trees below stay still
shortInsight: Weather is legible: wind, clouds and light each tell you what happens next.
physicalAction: Stand still and find the wind direction — use a leaf, grass, or your cheek. Then read the clouds for the next hour.
nextMission: Read the wind direction without any device.

note: air after rain, warm pavement and wet leaves
shortInsight: Air carries news: after rain, soil and leaves release a scent you can name without instruments.
physicalAction: Take one slow breath through your nose where you stand, then a few steps away. Is the air the same in both places?
nextMission: Find where the air smells different.

note: a place where one road sound keeps disappearing
shortInsight: Every place has a sound signature — most people never hear one twice.
physicalAction: Move ten steps toward the quietest direction and listen for ten seconds. Did any sound disappear? Did a new one arrive?
nextMission: Find where one sound disappears.

note: one minute of birdsong in a quiet corner
shortInsight: Recording changes nothing — until you play it back; your phone can hold one minute of this place.
physicalAction: Record one minute of standing still — and stand still the whole minute. Note what you only noticed during playback.
nextMission: Record one minute and find one sound you missed live.

note: three benches in a row, each used differently
shortInsight: The best discoveries usually arrive in threes — two more of the same property, not one of a kind.
physicalAction: Find two more things that share one property with what you noticed. Same colour? Same shape? Same sound?
nextMission: Find two more things sharing one property.

note: something small and bright moving at the edge of vision
shortInsight: Not knowing is the start, not the failure — observation beats identification.
physicalAction: Look again for thirty seconds and find one detail you can describe precisely without naming anything.
nextMission: Describe one detail precisely — no names allowed.
